The Canopy Line

A high‑resolution, pannable read of forest canopy cover along the Dominican Republic–Haiti border, where a single political line splits two starkly different landscapes — the Dominican Republic's protected mountain forests and Haiti's stripped, charcoal‑dependent hills. Scroll or drag to explore; the contrast is sharp enough to be visible from orbit.

How to read this

Use the Model / Satellite toggle above the map to check the composite against the real ground: satellite mode swaps in live aerial imagery (Esri World Imagery) under the same coastline and border, and once you're zoomed in far enough, a thin line outlines each individual model cell so you can compare its modeled canopy value directly against what's actually on the ground there — hover either mode for the per‑cell reading.

Each cell is a stylized pixel in a modeled tree‑canopy raster, rendered at roughly 0.3 map‑units per cell — a 4× jump in resolution over the initial version, so that zooming in close to the line shows real pixel grain instead of a smoothed gradient. Pale tan reads as bare or cleared ground, deep green as dense forest.

The coastline and border are no longer a hand‑traced approximation: both come from geoBoundaries.org's official Haiti and Dominican Republic boundary polygons, with the shared frontier extracted by finding where the two countries' independently‑surveyed outlines actually coincide — about 600 vertices tracing every real jog, including the westward turn around the Bassin Visite highlands that a straight line used to cut through. That same real border is what the model's sharp discontinuity is measured against. The one deliberate softening: the arid basin around Lake Enriquillo and Jimaní reads similarly dry on both sides here, since that stretch is naturally arid rather than a product of the border, so the model damps the political‑line effect there instead of overstating it.

The regional pattern — mountain ranges greener than valleys and cities on both sides — is built from real topography and known reserves, but the values themselves remain an illustrative composite for cartographic storytelling, not a calibrated satellite product. The border discontinuity itself is real: independent surveys (Landsat, MODIS, and Google Earth imagery going back to the iconic 2002 NASA photo) have documented an abrupt line in vegetation cover along the DR–Haiti frontier, though how dramatic it looks varies by segment and by year — current imagery in several stretches shows a softer edge than that 2002 photo, consistent with Haiti's tree cover (agroforestry included) recovering somewhat since then.

Why the line is there

The roots go back to independence: France recognized Haiti in 1825 only in exchange for a 90‑million‑franc indemnity, and 19th‑century Haitian governments paid much of it by exporting timber, stripping lowland forest decades before the Dominican side saw comparable pressure. Today Haiti relies on wood and charcoal for roughly three‑quarters of household energy, and decades of weak land tenure and park enforcement left little standing forest outside a handful of reserves like Macaya and La Visite. The Dominican Republic, by contrast, built a national park system and forestry controls from the 1930s onward, shifted rural energy toward propane, and has spent decades reforesting upland watersheds that feed its hydroelectric dams.

The often‑repeated statistic that Haiti has “2% forest cover” is contested — newer remote‑sensing work that counts agroforestry and tree crops puts Haiti's real tree cover meaningfully higher. But the direction of the gap, and its sharpness right at the border, is not in dispute.

Coastline and border: Haiti and Dominican Republic ADM0 boundaries via geoBoundaries.org (open, CC BY 4.0). The canopy grid remains a modeled composite for cartographic storytelling, informed by documented reserves and land‑use patterns rather than a primary remote‑sensing measurement.
